label: DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 1017
output:
**The Long Version**

Okay, group chat. Jess texted me last night—“It’s one assignment, don’t torch your job over it”—and half of you agreed with her, and I started typing a response and realized it was going to be fourteen texts and nobody needs that. So here’s the long version. Jess, this is mostly for you. Everyone else, sorry, you’re getting it too.

Here’s the assignment. My juniors, US History II, two sections. They interview someone in their family or neighborhood about Boston in 1974–76, during busing and desegregation. Ten-minute recording, two-page reflection. That’s it. I’ve run it for four years at Cobb Street and never had a complaint until now.

The complaint came as an email to Dr. Halvorsen, cc’ing a school committee member. The parent said the project “reopens wounds” and “pressures kids to judge their grandparents.” I read it twice. The first part I don’t buy. The second part I’ve been thinking about, because I actually think she has a point. Not the whole point, but a point.

I have a meeting with Halvorsen and the parent on Thursday, November 19, at 3:15. My plan is not to quietly drop it. My plan is to keep the assignment and add an alternate option—interview a librarian or archivist, or use recorded interviews from past years with permission—so no kid has to interview family. No questions asked. Same skills, same reflection, different source. If the problem is pressure, I can fix the pressure. If the problem is the history itself, that’s a different conversation.

I’m not going into Thursday to pick a fight with this parent. I don’t know her. I believe her that she’s worried about her kid. I don’t think she’s a villain. I think she’s wrong about the assignment being dropped, but I don’t think she’s wrong that a kid can feel put in the position of judging Grandma. That’s a real thing, and I can design around it.

What I can’t do is pretend the assignment is some radical thing. It’s local history. It’s the history of the city they live in. The textbook gives it one paragraph and moves on. Four years of kids have come back from these interviews with something the textbook can’t give them, which is the feeling that history happened here, to people they know, and that those people are complicated.

The one I keep thinking about is D. in 2023. He interviewed his grandmother, who drove a school bus in Southie in ’74. She had never told anyone in the family. Not anyone. He played forty seconds of the recording for the class and nobody said a word for about a minute. Not because it was dramatic. Because it was real and it was in the room. I’ve been teaching long enough to know you can’t manufacture that.

Then last year a girl found out her uncle threw rocks at a bus. She was upset. We talked after class twice. I’m not going to pretend I handled it perfectly or that it was easy for her. But her reflection was the best thing I read all year. She didn’t write a neat little lesson. She wrote about how she loved her uncle and thought what he did was wrong and didn’t know what to do with both of those things at once. That’s not me pressing a kid to judge her family. That’s a kid finding out her family is full of people who made choices, like everybody’s family.

I keep coming back to something I believe but don’t know how to say without sounding like a sermon: the kids who get uncomfortable in this unit are often the ones for whom the history has suddenly become real. But I don’t get to force anyone into that. That’s the line. My job is to make a room where they can ask the question, not to push them out of a moving car.

Jess, I know what you meant. We met student teaching in 2012 at the same school. You left teaching in 2019 and now you do HR at a biotech in Cambridge, and you have a much clearer view than I do of how institutions protect themselves. You’re not wrong that I could get burned. I’m not untenured—I’ve been tenured since 2021—but Halvorsen still controls my schedule and who gets AP, and I’m not naive about what it means to be the person who won’t let something go. I don’t want to find out how much that costs.

And I’m not writing this because I’m brave. I’m a little scared, honestly. I don’t like this kind of conflict. I’d rather be grading. I’m not trying to be a martyr over one assignment. I just don’t think “one assignment” is the right way to see it. If I drop this because one parent sent an email, then the next weird email decides what I teach. That’s the part I can’t get past. Not because I’m on some crusade, but because I’ve been doing this long enough to know that the quiet version of dropping it is how a lot of good stuff disappears.

I don’t need you to agree with me. I really don’t. I want you to understand why I’m not deleting it. I get why you said what you said. If I were you, watching from outside teaching, I might have sent the same text. I’m not mad. I just didn’t want to argue in fifteen texts, so here’s the whole thing once.

I’ll text you Thursday after the meeting. Probably from the parking lot, probably before I even turn the key. Even if it’s just “well, that happened.”
